source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: Large text-trained LMs used as arithmetic-coding compressors beat domain-specific compressors on images and audio. This is the strongest evidence that a good predictor is a good approximation to K.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B: ImageNet patches 43.4% of raw size (PNG 58.5%); LibriSpeech 16.4% (FLAC 30.3%). On enwik9 raw rate 8.3% for Chinchilla 70B; adjusted for parameter size 21.9%.
quote: Chinchilla 70B, trained primarily on text, compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4%
limits: Raw rates ignore model size. Once the weights are counted (two-part code) the big models lose on small data. Transformers trained only on enwik8 overfit to Wikipedia and compress other modalities poorly.
agent_relevance: Compression power comes from the predictor, not from a short explicit program; weights are the hidden cost. Our scaffold has no weights to count, so rule length must be judged in prompt tokens.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression (adjusted rates)
finding: When model size is added to the code length (the honest K upper bound), large LMs gain only on big text sets and lose on other data.
numbers: Adjusted compression rate: Chinchilla 70B 21.9% on enwik9 versus gzip 32.3%; on ImageNet, LibriSpeech and random data the adjusted rates for Chinchilla 70B are about 185%, 229% and 225%, worse than the raw data.
limits: Only a 1GB text set offsets the cost of a 70B model. The adjusted figures are read from a table with garbled layout; check against the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: Shortest-description comparisons must charge for the description of the model or rule itself (two-part code), not only for the fit. This fits G3 held-out checks plus a length charge on the rule.

source: Huang, Zhang, Shan, He (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly
finding: Across many public LLMs, bits per character on fresh external text correlates almost linearly with average benchmark score.
numbers: 31 public LLMs, 12 benchmarks (knowledge, coding, math). Pearson about -0.95 per domain; overall -0.93 with RMSE 3.1%.
limits: Only well-trained base models; the authors say it may not hold for LMs not trained to convergence. The correlation is clearly weaker with out-of-domain corpora. Some benchmark points are outliers (likely overfit to benchmarks). Benchmarks near saturation behave differently.
agent_relevance: Compression of the target domain predicts ability in that domain; a length score is a sound ranking signal across models, but a weaker signal across domains.

source: Xuyang et al. (2025) Is Compression Really Linear with Code Intelligence?
finding: Partial failed replication of the linearity claim in the code domain. A preliminary run showed no clear correlation; with a new unseen GitHub validation set and a fine-tuning step called Format Annealing the relation is logarithmic, not linear.
numbers: Code BPC vs log-transformed code intelligence: Pearson -0.956, RMSE 5.7% on the open-source validation set; -0.956 with RMSE 9% on the closed-source set. Linearity seen earlier is described as the tail of a log curve.
limits: Per-language correlation differs: SQL is worse than Python because pretraining data is Python-heavy. Needs multi-task averaging. Depends on Format Annealing.
agent_relevance: Compression is a ranking signal with diminishing returns at the high-BPC end; small differences between good models may mean little.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation
finding: Direct test of LLMs as shortest-program finders. Flagship LLMs fail to produce a correct program for most natural sequences.
numbers: Sequences of 128 bytes. Accuracy (program reproduces input exactly) GPT-4o: audio-16bit 35.6%, audio-8bit 15.0%, MFCC 29.6%, DNA 24.8%, text 6.5%, synthetic 33.3%. Llama-3.1-405B: 18.0, 10.1, 24.2, 22.5, 9.6, 18.0. Llama-3.1-8B: 5.9, 3.9, 8.8, 3.7, 1.4, 8.5. Programs fail to reproduce the input more than 78% (Llama-405B) and 40% (GPT-4o) of the time on natural data (paper wording).
limits: Precision (program length relative to gzip) of prompted models is above 1.5 in every cell, so even correct programs are longer than gzip output. Chain of thought changed accuracy by -1.3 and -5.1 points for 8B and 70B and +2.1 for 405B.
agent_relevance: For our S7 shortest-rule step: LLMs can often write a rule that fits, but it is rarely shorter than a generic compressor would give. Do not trust the model's own claim that its rule is shortest; count the length.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation (trained SeqCoder)
finding: Training on synthetic program-sequence pairs gives strong in-distribution compression but does not transfer to real data.
numbers: SeqCoder-1.5B: synthetic accuracy 44.7% at length 128, precision 1.65; larger trained model 84.5 to 92.5% synthetic accuracy with precision 0.56-0.57 (better than gzip). Real data: 0.0 to 0.1% for the larger trained models on audio, DNA and text. Length-64 test: 86.6% synthetic vs 6.5% real MFCC.
limits: Models trained on 10K to 1M synthetic pairs. For 10K-trained models more than 99% of programs fail in the first 16 characters on audio MFCC. Execution feedback gave small gains on real data (6.5 to 8.7%).
agent_relevance: Learned simplicity priors are tied to the generating distribution; a shortest-rule preference is only as good as the match between prior and task.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation (repetition shortcut)
finding: Most correct programs on natural data just copy the input (repetition), so success is not real compression.
numbers: Manual check of 25 correct programs per modality: repetition accounts for more than 95% of correct predictions on natural data, about 20% on synthetic data. gzip compression rate on Audio-8bit: 0.966 (len 16), 0.846 (32), 0.736 (64), 0.622 (128), 0.398 (1M). Llama-405B accuracy at lengths 16/32/64/128: 47.1, 29.9, 20.9, 14.2%.
limits: Small qualitative sample (25 per modality).
agent_relevance: A reward on length must reject trivial 'print the data' rules; check that the rule is shorter than the data it explains (ratio under 1).

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor
finding: Shows next-token loss of an in-context learner equals prequential code length, an upper bound on K(D), so ICL implicitly trades off fit against model complexity.
numbers: Meta-learned prequential ICL generalises better than train-risk ICL and than SGD-fitted MLPs in low-data regimes across tasks. With enough data SGD matches it, and on Mastermind does better. L2 and other regularised SGD are still beaten by prequential ICL in low-data regimes. Training on only the latter half of the sequence gives worse prequential code length.
limits: GPT-4 on novel Mastermind tasks does far worse than small meta-trained ICL models and a naive marginal-class baseline (5 seeds). Large pretrained models can fail to minimise prequential code length on new tasks.
agent_relevance: Occam preference helps most when examples are few, as in our per-problem scaffold; it adds little when data is plentiful.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Learning Universal Predictors
finding: Neural nets trained on data from random programs on a universal Turing machine (BrainPhoque) learn Solomonoff-like prediction and transfer to other tasks.
numbers: Larger models predict better on UTM data. On variable-order Markov sources, Transformer-L and LSTM-L match the optimal CTW predictor. LSTMs generalise to longer sequences (1024 steps) better than Transformers. Evaluated on 15 Chomsky-hierarchy tasks with transfer.
limits: Results depend on the chosen UTM and on small models. Solomonoff induction itself is approached, not reached.
agent_relevance: Amortised Solomonoff induction is a training idea; a scaffold can only rank candidate rules by explicit length.

source: Goldblum, Finzi, Rowan, Wilson (2024) The No Free Lunch Theorem, Kolmogorov Complexity, and the Role of Inductive Biases
finding: LMs, even randomly initialised GPT-2, give higher probability to low-complexity sequences, as the Solomonoff prior would. Bigger GPT-3 variants show it more.
numbers: GPT-3 Ada, Babbage, Curie, Davinci tested on sequences from short binary expression trees: log-probability falls with minimum complexity (bits), strongest for Davinci. Pretrained GPT-2 shows a stronger low-complexity preference than random GPT-2. Neural nets compress labels of CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, FMNIST.
limits: Complexity measured with a restricted expression-tree language, not true K. The effect is a preference, not a guarantee; average completion accuracy over all length-10 bitstrings stays 0.5.
agent_relevance: LLMs already carry a built-in simplicity prior, so asking for the simplest rule uses a bias that exists; it is architectural and cannot be tuned by prompting.

source: Gauvrit, Zenil, Delahaye, Soler-Toscano (2014) Algorithmic complexity for short binary strings applied to psychology
finding: The Coding Theorem Method gives a K-like score (K5) for strings of length 50 or less, where standard K and compression are not usable. It disagrees with entropy.
numbers: '010101010101' has K5 = 26.99 and '100101110001' has K5 = 36.06, both with maximum entropy. '110011011111' has entropy 0.811 but K5 33.36, higher than the alternating string. All strings with H<0.5 have low K5.
limits: Values depend on the reference machine (D(5), 5-state 2-symbol machines). Binary strings only.
agent_relevance: Short observation lists in a scaffold are in the regime where gzip-style compression is useless; use explicit rule length, not compressed size.

source: Gauvrit et al. (2014) children's random string production (experiment in the same paper)
finding: Children aged 7 to 11 produce strings more complex than a uniform random draw, so people aim for mild complexity rather than sampling uniformly.
numbers: N = 68 children (mean age 8.7, SD 1.1), grades 2 to 4, length-8 strings. Mean K5 of children 21.74 (SD 0.52) vs random strings 21.46; t(67) = 4.35, p < 5e-5. Grade effect not significant: F(2,65) = 0.68, eta squared = 0.11.
limits: Single study, no replication found in this session; small effect across grades; binary strings only.
agent_relevance: Human 'looks random' judgements track algorithmic complexity but overshoot; a rule-length score and human intuition can disagree.

source: Gauvrit, Soler-Toscano, Zenil (2015) Natural scene statistics mediate the perception of image complexity
finding: Reanalysis of Hsu et al. 2010 plus a new experiment. Human randomness judgments of 2D arrays track algorithmic complexity but natural-world frequency explains more, so K is not the whole account.
numbers: Hsu data (100 arrays, 77 raters): algorithmic complexity vs subjective randomness r = .52; natural statistics vs subjective r = .75; regression adj R2 = .58, coefficients complexity .19 (p = .013) vs natural stats .66; Sobel z = 4.78. New experiment N = 100 MTurk: complexity-subjective r = .36, natural-subjective r = .56, adj R2 = .31, Sobel z = 3.66.
limits: Complexity measure is an approximation (CTM for 2D); online sample; perception only.
agent_relevance: A shortest-description score captures only part of what people call simple; learned frequency (a prior) also matters. For the agent: add a prior from past cases, not just length.

source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2003) From Algorithmic to Subjective Randomness; Griffiths et al. (2018) Subjective randomness as statistical inference
finding: Seen only in search results. They argue algorithmic complexity is incomputable and too general to capture the regularities people see; a model-selection (Bayesian) account does better.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Search snippets only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a restricted rule language with a prior, not an unrestricted shortest program.

source: Feldman (2000) Minimization of Boolean complexity in human concept learning (Nature)
finding: Search result states parsimony as minimisation of complexity may play a role in human category learning. Exact results not read.
numbers: Not opened; no figures.
limits: Known from search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Founding human evidence for the shortest-rule preference.

source: Lafond, Lacouture, Mineau (2007) Complexity minimization in rule-based category learning
finding: Title says they revised the catalogue of Boolean concepts and found evidence for non-minimal rules, i.e. people do not always use the shortest rule. Content not read.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Only bibliographic details seen; claim inferred from the title, unverified.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the shortest rule is the one people (or the best agent) use.

source: Pape, Kurtz, Sayama (2015) Complexity Measures and Concept Learning
finding: Rival to Boolean-complexity (shortest rule) accounts. Logical complexity explains one difficulty ordering of six category types (paradigm-specific) but not the general ordering seen with non-separable stimuli, children and monkeys; a Shannon-entropy measure explains both.
numbers: u-min (minimal uncertainty) predicts the paradigm-specific order; u-mean (average uncertainty) predicts the general order with correlation about 0.97. Beyond the six types u-min predicts as well or better than Boolean complexity and GISTM in most cases (GISTM wins on 4[2]).
limits: Fit on two classic datasets (Nosofsky et al. 1994, 1996) plus extrapolation. Kurtz et al. 2013 (cited): instructions to look for rules produced the rule-based Type II advantage, neutral instructions did not.
agent_relevance: Moderator: rule-seeking instructions switch on shortest-rule behaviour, and it fits separable features only. Telling the model to look for a rule may be the lever.

source: Zenil (2020) A Review of Methods for Estimating Algorithmic Complexity
finding: Lists estimators: statistical compression (LZW, gzip), Coding Theorem Method (CTM), Block Decomposition Method (BDM). Argues compression is an entropy-rate estimator no closer to K than Shannon entropy, and that CTM/BDM complement it for short strings.
numbers: No benchmark number. Claims CTM beats compression for short strings and compression suits long strings. Written as a rebuttal to a minireview by Vitanyi (its content not read).
limits: Author developed CTM/BDM, a conflict of interest; the dispute with Vitanyi is not settled in this source.
agent_relevance: Estimator choice matters by length regime; compare rules from one family with the same estimator.

source: Zenil et al. (2018) A decomposition method for global evaluation of Shannon entropy and local estimations of algorithmic complexity
finding: BDM sums CTM values of blocks. It behaves like Shannon entropy when it loses accuracy and equals CTM for small objects.
numbers: Spearman test between BDM and CTM on the first 4096 binary strings: p < 1e-15. For block size above 6, BDM rank correlation with CTM is higher than CTM versus entropy or compression.
limits: Accuracy drops as blocks get small; no independent critique found this session.
agent_relevance: Estimators track true K only by rank and only for small objects; use them for ordering only.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: A 76K-parameter network with no pretraining minimises description length of each puzzle at test time and solves a fifth of ARC-AGI-1 evaluation puzzles.
numbers: 20% on 400 public evaluation puzzles (2 guesses), 34.75% on 400 training puzzles. 2000 steps, about 20 minutes per puzzle. Training set pass@1 30.25%, pass@2 34.75%, pass@1000 52.75%. ARC-AGI-2 about 4% (third-party summary, not verified).
quote: solves 20% of evaluation puzzles by minimizing the description length
limits: Fails on long-range pattern extension and other abilities listed in its Appendix H. Far below LLM systems (o3 high 87.5% on semi-private eval at high compute).
agent_relevance: Strongest positive evidence that MDL selection works as a solver, but it needs gradient steps and compute, not a prompt scaffold.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: an MDL-based framework for program synthesis in ARC
finding: MDL-guided program synthesis for ARC is efficient and interpretable but scores below LLM approaches.
numbers: 7% at ArcPrize 2024, up from 2% at ARCathon 2022. 80% of solutions found in the first 20 s. Generalisation rate of found solutions about 82%.
limits: Results table text is garbled by extraction, so per-split figures are omitted.
agent_relevance: MDL ranks candidates; the candidate generator is the bottleneck. Spend effort on candidate rules, then rank by length.

source: Sun & Saparov (2025) Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor?
finding: On synthetic first-order-logic induction and abduction, LLMs reach correct hypotheses but rarely the simplest ones.
numbers: Height-1 ontologies: all models above 80% weak and strong accuracy. Multi-hypothesis: accuracy falls from above 80% to below 50% from height 1 to 2 for all models except GPT-4o. At height 4, weak accuracy at least 20% but quality and strong accuracy very low. GPT-5.4 and o3 beat Llama3-70B; buffer-of-thought beats chain of thought. SFT of Qwen3-4B adds +1.5% (height 4) to +11.0% (height 1) strong accuracy. Human-validated metric agreement 79% vs 33.3% chance and 51% for a length heuristic.
limits: Synthetic ontology data in first-order logic; transfer to real tasks unclear (authors).
agent_relevance: Models need an explicit minimality check; weak accuracy hides unnecessary hypotheses. Count hypotheses and reward fewer.

source: Wan & Mei (2025) LLMs as Computable Approximations to Solomonoff Induction
finding: Theory paper claiming training approximates the Solomonoff prior; a few-shot selection rule that picks low-confidence examples improves small models.
numbers: Text-classification experiments report significant gains mostly for smaller models; exact figures not extracted.
limits: Theoretical claims, not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Low-confidence example selection is a cheap scaffold-compatible idea; evidence is thin.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Unifying Two Types of Scaling Laws from Conditional Kolmogorov Complexity
finding: Theory: conditional K bounds what an LLM can solve; more execution steps (longer chain of thought) approximate it better.
numbers: No empirical numbers read; states infinitely many problems cannot be solved by models.
limits: Theory only; read as an argument, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Supports spending more tokens on search before committing to a short rule, only as an argument.

source: Li & Vitanyi (2008) An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications
finding: Standard reference cited by the papers read for the invariance theorem and the link of MDL to K. Not opened.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background for: K is uncomputable and defined only up to a constant.

source: Synthesis: short strings and constants
finding: K is defined up to a machine-dependent constant; for short inputs this dominates, so 'shortest' holds only inside a fixed language.
numbers: Gauvrit: standard K inapplicable to strings of length 50 or less. Yoran: gzip rate 0.966 at 16 bytes versus 0.398 at 1M bytes.
limits: Synthesis of b11 and b07.
agent_relevance: Fix the rule language once and compare lengths only within it.

source: Synthesis: what interventions changed performance
finding: Scale (Llama 8B to 405B about tripled accuracy), synthetic training (in-distribution only), SFT on parsimony data (+1.5 to +11 points) and meta-training for prequential code (better at low data) helped. Chain of thought (mixed), execution feedback (small) and regularised SGD did not clearly help.
limits: Different tasks and metrics; not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone has no measured effect on shortest-rule quality; selection by an external length count is the safest lever.
